advances: The original volume law admits both requested centered moment estimates for every deterministic centroid matrix, including dense matrices of full column rank. The second-moment constant is 25/8. The fourth-moment constant can be taken to be 10^10, independently of the radius, the lattice dimensions, and the row coefficients. The proof establishes nonpositive coordinate covariances directly, proves the one-dimensional log-concavity input and its fourth-moment consequence, and uses exact shell convolutions at the original weights. The fourth-moment bound gives an inward-coordinate fit on almost all original volume as n grows, even when d=n. A separate cube-cap estimate at a bounded Euclidean offset with a fixed coordinate margin remains the precise bridge to a depth conclusion; this packet does not assert that conclusion.

proof:
Write \(X=|Z|\) and \(L=\sum_iX_i\). These are abbreviations for the coordinatewise absolute-value vector and its sum; Z retains its lattice-vector meaning. The upper fiber constraint for row l is
\(y_l\le R-\sum_i(1-B_{li})|x_i|\), whose right side is concave because every coefficient \(1-B_{li}\) is nonnegative. The lower constraint is \(y_l\ge-R+\sum_i(1+B_{li})|x_i|\), whose right side is convex. Together with \(\sum_i|x_i|\le R\), these epigraph and hypograph constraints prove convexity. They are closed, and they imply \(|x_i|\le R\) and \(-R\le y_l\le R\), so the body is compact. All constraints are strict at \((0_n,0_d)\); continuity gives an ambient open neighborhood in the body. Taking integer fibers proves their stated shapes and volumes. Boundary fibers have zero d-dimensional volume. The finite set D_+ contains 0_n, so every partition function used below is positive. Its convex hull has l_1 norm strictly below R, proving completeness of the positive integer support as well.

First establish the covariance claim without invoking negative association. Fix k>0 and two distinct coordinates i,j. If X_i=t is in its conditional support, the conditional distribution of the remaining total \(L-X_i=s\) is proportional to \(A_{n-1}(s)(R-t-s)^k\) for integers \(0\le s<R-t\), where \(A_m(s)\) counts signed lattice vectors of l_1 norm s in dimension m. For \(t_2>t_1\), the ratio of these two unnormalized conditional weights is
\(r(s)=[(R-t_2-s)_+/(R-t_1-s)]^k\) on the support for t_1. This is nonincreasing in s, including where its numerator becomes zero. Under the t_1 law, the difference between the two conditional means of s equals \(\operatorname{Cov}(s,r(s))/\mathbb E r(s)\), which is nonpositive. Indeed, for any variable Y and functions f,g, independent copies Y,Y' give
\(2\operatorname{Cov}(f(Y),g(Y))=\mathbb E[(f(Y)-f(Y'))(g(Y)-g(Y'))]\); oppositely monotone functions give a nonpositive product. Exchangeability of the remaining n-1 coordinates gives \(\mathbb E[X_j\mid X_i=t]=\mathbb E[L-X_i\mid X_i=t]/(n-1)\). This conditional mean is nonincreasing in t. The same covariance identity now proves \(\operatorname{Cov}_{q^{(k)}}(X_i,X_j)\le0\).

Let \(v_k=\operatorname{Var}_{q^{(k)}}X_1\), and let \(c_k\) be the common covariance of distinct coordinates. Exchangeability makes the covariance matrix have diagonal v_k and off-diagonal c_k. Its eigenvalues are \(v_k-c_k\) on the subspace orthogonal to \(\mathbf1_n\), and \(v_k+(n-1)c_k\) in the direction \(\mathbf1_n\). Positivity and c_k<=0 imply

\[
\lambda_{\max}(\operatorname{Cov}_{q^{(k)}}X)
 =v_k-c_k\le\frac n{n-1}v_k
 \le\frac n{n-1}\mathbb E_{q^{(k)}}X_1^2,
\qquad
\operatorname{Var}_{q^{(k)}}L\le n\mathbb E_{q^{(k)}}X_1^2.
\tag{1}
\]

The second-moment assertion in accepted fact 5e81b94633eacd39 and coordinate symmetry give
\((\mathcal Z_{d-2}/\mathcal Z_d)\mathbb E_{q^{(d-2)}}X_1^2\le2/[d(d-1)]\). This is an assertion about exactly the same radial lattice weights; no property of that fact's special centroid is being transferred to c_B. Centering at mu and applying (1) yields

\[
\begin{aligned}
\mathbb E_p\frac{\|B(X-\mu)\|_2^2}{a_Z^2}
&=\frac{\mathcal Z_{d-2}}{\mathcal Z_d}
 \operatorname{tr}\!\left(B\operatorname{Cov}_{q^{(d-2)}}(X)B^{\mathsf T}\right)\\
&\le\frac{2n}{(n-1)d(d-1)}\|B\|_F^2
\le\frac{2n^2}{(n-1)(d-1)}
\le\frac{25}{8}\frac nd.
\end{aligned}
\tag{2}
\]

The last inequality uses n,d>=5, and the preceding one uses \(\|B\|_F^2\le dn\).

Here are two elementary log-concavity facts needed for the fourth moment, with proofs. A nonnegative sequence with interval support is called log-concave when \(u_j^2\ge u_{j-1}u_{j+1}\). Convolution preserves this property. To verify that statement directly, the decreasing ratios of a log-concave sequence imply that all two-by-two minors of its Toeplitz matrix \((u_{i-j})_{i,j\in\mathbb Z}\) are nonnegative: the two diagonal indices are between the off-diagonal indices and have the same sum, so the product at the inner indices is at least the product at the outer indices. If an outer value is zero the inequality is automatic; otherwise all intervening values are positive and the ratio argument applies. The product of two such Toeplitz matrices is the Toeplitz matrix of their convolution. For any selected two rows and two columns, expansion of its determinant expresses it as the sum, over pairs of intermediate indices, of the products of the corresponding two-by-two minors of the factors. Every summand is nonnegative. For finite-support sequences this is a finite identity; truncation proves every coefficient needed from an infinite-support sequence. Taking adjacent rows and columns proves convolution log-concavity, and interval support is preserved by convolution.

Second, a finite-support integer-valued variable V with log-concave mass function satisfies

\[
\mathbb E|V-\mathbb EV|^4
 \le20000\left((\operatorname{Var}V)^2+\operatorname{Var}V\right).
\tag{3}
\]

For a complete proof, let V' be an independent copy, D=V-V', and \(v=\mathbb E D^2=2\operatorname{Var}V\). The mass function \(t_j=\mathbb P(D=j)\) is symmetric and log-concave by the convolution fact just proved. The mass function of |D| is \(u_0=t_0\) and \(u_j=2t_j\) for j>=1. It is log-concave: at j=1 use \(4t_1^2\ge2t_0t_2\), and at all larger indices use the log-concavity of t. If D is identically zero, (3) follows immediately. Otherwise let \(T_j=\mathbb P(|D|\ge j)\), with T_0=1. These tails are log-concave. Indeed, on their positive support the ratios \(u_{j+r}/u_j\) are nonincreasing in j for each r>=0, so \(T_j/u_j\) is nonincreasing. Consequently \(T_{j+1}/T_j=1-u_j/T_j\) is nonincreasing. In particular, \(T_j\le T_1^j\) and \(T_{mJ}\le T_J^m\) for nonnegative integers m and positive integers J.

The exact tail identity is \(\mathbb E D^4=\sum_{j\ge1}(j^4-(j-1)^4)T_j\). If 0<v<=1/4, then T_1<=v and the geometric-series identity gives
\(\mathbb E D^4\le4\sum_{j\ge1}j^3v^j=4v(1+4v+v^2)/(1-v)^4\le27v\). If v>1/4, put \(J=\lceil2\sqrt v\rceil\le4\sqrt v\). Markov's inequality gives T_J<=1/4. Grouping the tail identity into consecutive blocks of length J gives
\(\mathbb E D^4\le J^4\sum_{m\ge0}(m+1)^4 4^{-m}<19J^4\le4864v^2\). The displayed series is less than 19 because it equals \((1+11/4+11/16+1/64)/(1-1/4)^5=4560/243\); the earlier cubic-series identity follows by differentiating the geometric series. Thus in both cases \(\mathbb ED^4\le5000(v^2+v)\). Jensen's inequality conditional on V gives \(\mathbb E|V-\mathbb EV|^4\le\mathbb E|V-V'|^4\). Substitution of v=2 Var V proves (3).

For the radial lattice law q^(k), the law of L has mass proportional to \(A_n(s)(R-s)^k\), for integers 0<=s<R. This mass function is log-concave. A single absolute coordinate has counting sequence 1,2,2,..., which is log-concave. Its n-fold convolution is A_n. One may truncate the coordinate sequence after \(\lceil R\rceil-1\) before using the convolution proof, since coefficients with s<R are unchanged. The sequence \((R-s)^k\) on this interval is log-concave because \(k\log(R-s)\) is concave. The product of two nonnegative log-concave sequences with interval support is log-concave. Consequently (3), (1), and the integer inequalities \(\mathbb EX_1^2\le\mathbb EX_1^4\) and \((\mathbb EX_1^2)^2\le\mathbb EX_1^4\) give

\[
\mathbb E_{q^{(k)}}|L-\mathbb E_{q^{(k)}}L|^4
 \le40000n^2\mathbb E_{q^{(k)}}X_1^4.
\tag{4}
\]

The first of the two integer inequalities uses X_1 in the nonnegative integers; the second is Cauchy-Schwarz. Thus the possible small-variance lattice regime has not been suppressed by an unsupported kurtosis bound.

We next control all directions orthogonal to the all-ones vector without a negative-association assertion. In any exchangeable nonnegative n-vector X, put \(m_4=\mathbb EX_1^4\), \(m_{31}=\mathbb EX_1^3X_2\), \(m_{22}=\mathbb EX_1^2X_2^2\), \(m_{211}=\mathbb EX_1^2X_2X_3\), and \(m_{1111}=\mathbb EX_1X_2X_3X_4\). All these are between zero and m_4 by the arithmetic-geometric mean inequality and exchangeability. For any real vector h with sum_i h_i=0, let \(A_2=\sum_i h_i^2\) and \(A_4=\sum_i h_i^4\). Expansion of the fourth power, with sums over distinct indices ordered, gives

\[
\begin{aligned}
\mathbb E(h\cdot X)^4
={}&A_4(m_4-4m_{31}-3m_{22}+12m_{211}-6m_{1111})\\
 &+A_2^2(3m_{22}-6m_{211}+3m_{1111})
 \le38 A_2^2m_4.
\end{aligned}
\tag{5}
\]

For explicit verification of the coefficient cancellations, the sums for the exponent patterns 31, 22, 211, and 1111 are respectively \(-A_4\), \(A_2^2-A_4\), \(2A_4-A_2^2\), and \(3A_2^2-6A_4\). Their multinomial coefficients in the ordered expansion are 4,3,6,1. The absolute sums of coefficients in the two parentheses in (5) are 26 and 12, and A_4<=A_2^2, proving the stated bound.

Let \(\mu^{(k)}=\mathbb E_{q^{(k)}}X\). For arbitrary b put \(\bar b=n^{-1}\sum_i b_i\) and \(h=b-\bar b\mathbf1_n\). Exchangeability gives \(b\cdot(X-\mu^{(k)})=h\cdot X+\bar b(L-\mathbb EL)\). Moreover, \(\sum h_i^2\le\sum b_i^2\), and \(\bar b^4 n^2\le(\sum b_i^2)^2\). Using \((u+v)^4\le8(u^4+v^4)\), (4), and (5), we obtain for every k>0

\[
\mathbb E_{q^{(k)}}[b\cdot(X-\mu^{(k)})]^4
 \le320304\left(\sum_i b_i^2\right)^2
       \mathbb E_{q^{(k)}}X_1^4.
\tag{6}
\]

We now prove the two exact radial shell comparisons used to transfer (6) to the requested centering and original law. All generating series in this argument are formal. The single-coordinate counting series is \(M(t)=(1+t)/(1-t)\). Differentiating it gives

\[
\begin{aligned}
\sum_{s\ge0}sA_n(s)t^s
 &=\frac{2nt}{1-t^2}\sum_{s\ge0}A_n(s)t^s,\\
\sum_{s\ge0}\left(\sum_{\|z\|_1=s}|z_1|^4\right)t^s
 &=\frac{2t(1+10t+t^2)}{(1-t)^4}
       \sum_{s\ge0}A_n(s)t^s,\\
\frac{2t(1+10t+t^2)}{(1-t)^4}
 &=\sum_{j\ge1}(4j^3-2j)t^j.
\end{aligned}
\tag{7}
\]

For the second line, applying \((t\,d/dt)^4\) to \(\sum_{j\ge0}t^j\) and multiplying by 2 gives the signed fourth-moment single-coordinate series \(2t(1+11t+11t^2+t^3)/(1-t)^5\). Dividing by M(t) yields the displayed factor. Expanding \((1-t)^{-4}\) verifies the last line coefficientwise.

If k>=1 and b_0>0, the function \(u\mapsto(b_0-u)_+^k\) is convex. The midpoint inequality on each interval [2j,2j+2] therefore gives
\(2\sum_{j\ge0}(b_0-2j-1)_+^k\le\int_0^\infty(b_0-u)_+^k\,du=b_0^{k+1}/(k+1)\). The first convolution identity in (7) now implies

\[
\mathbb E_{q^{(k)}}L
 \le\frac n{k+1}\frac{\mathcal Z_{k+1}}{\mathcal Z_k}
 =\frac n{k+1}\mathbb E_{q^{(k)}}a_Z,
\qquad
\mathbb E_{q^{(k)}}a_Z\ge\frac{k+1}{n+k+1}R.
\tag{8}
\]

The second inequality follows from the identity L+a_Z=R.

For the fourth-moment comparison, the function \((u_1,u_2,u_3,u_4)\mapsto(b_0-\sum_r u_r)_+^k\) is convex when k>=1. Partition the nonnegative orthant into cubes of side 1/2. Every cube has volume 1/16, and convexity makes its integral at least 1/16 times its value at the center. Centers with sum equal to the positive integer j correspond exactly to four nonnegative integer indices with sum 2j-2, of which there are \(\binom{2j+1}{3}\). Since \(3\binom{2j+1}{3}=4j^3-j\ge4j^3-2j\), retaining just those centers gives the exact inequality

\[
\begin{aligned}
\sum_{j\ge1}(4j^3-2j)(b_0-j)_+^k
&\le48\int_{[0,\infty)^4}(b_0-u_1-u_2-u_3-u_4)_+^k\,du\\
&=\frac{48b_0^{k+4}}{(k+1)(k+2)(k+3)(k+4)}.
\end{aligned}
\tag{9}
\]

The omitted centers have nonnegative values. Successive integration gives the last equality. Applying the fourth-moment convolution in (7) and (9) with b_0=R-s proves

\[
\frac{\mathcal Z_k}{\mathcal Z_{k+4}}
 \mathbb E_{q^{(k)}}X_1^4
 \le\frac{48}{(k+1)(k+2)(k+3)(k+4)}
 \qquad(k\ge1).
\tag{10}
\]

All shell sums that survive in (8) and (10) are finite. A shell at s=R has zero contribution, because all exponents here are positive. These arguments use no rounding of R and no asymptotic approximation.

Take k=d-4>=1. Equation (8) and d>=n>=5 give \(\mathbb E_{q^{(k)}}a_Z\ge2R/7\). Thus the exact density ratio between q^(k+2) and q^(k) satisfies
\(q_z^{(k+2)}/q_z^{(k)}=a_z^2/\mathbb E_{q^{(k)}}a_Z^2\le49/4\), where Jensen's inequality bounds the denominator below by \((2R/7)^2\). Let \(Y=b\cdot(X-\mu^{(k)})\). Since mu is exactly mu^(k+2), Jensen's inequality and this density bound show
\(|b\cdot(\mu-\mu^{(k)})|^4=|\mathbb E_{q^{(k+2)}}Y|^4\le(49/4)\mathbb E_{q^{(k)}}Y^4\). Therefore

\[
\mathbb E_{q^{(k)}}[b\cdot(X-\mu)]^4
 \le106\mathbb E_{q^{(k)}}Y^4.
\tag{11}
\]

Combining (6), (10), and (11), while retaining the original p weights, gives

\[
\begin{aligned}
\mathbb E_p\left(\frac{b\cdot(X-\mu)}{a_Z}\right)^4
&=\frac{\mathcal Z_{d-4}}{\mathcal Z_d}
       \mathbb E_{q^{(d-4)}}[b\cdot(X-\mu)]^4\\
&\le\frac{106\cdot320304\cdot48}{d(d-1)(d-2)(d-3)}
       \left(\sum_i b_i^2\right)^2\\
&\le\frac{10^{10}}{d^4}\left(\sum_i b_i^2\right)^2.
\end{aligned}
\tag{12}
\]

For the last inequality, d>=5 implies \(48d^4/[d(d-1)(d-2)(d-3)]\le250\), and \(106\cdot320304\cdot250=8488056000<10^{10}\). This proves the fourth estimate for every real b, so no randomness or coefficient restriction was used in its directional proof.

For the stated fit probabilities, every row b_l of B has \(\sum_i B_{li}^2\le n\). The fourth-moment Markov inequality and the union bound give
\(p(D_+\setminus F_B)\le16\sum_{l=1}^d\mathbb E_p[(b_l\cdot(X-\mu)/a_Z)^4]\le16\cdot10^{10}n^2/d^3\). Equation (2) similarly gives \(p(D_+\setminus G_B)\le n/(8d)\). Intersecting the two events and using nonnegativity of their masses proves the displayed positive-part bounds. On F_B the coordinate offsets from the actual centroid are at most a_z/2, so the fit is at least a_z/2 from every facet. Dividing by T_z=2a_z I_d gives maximum absolute normalized coordinate at most 1/4, and on G_B the normalized Euclidean norm is at most 5/2. Finally \(|(B\mu)_l|\le\sum_i\mu_i=\mathbb E_{q^{(d-2)}}L<R\), so \((0_n,B\mu)\) lies in the origin fiber regardless of the fit events.

To specify what remains for a depth argument, the small-offset cube-cap calculation of accepted fact 5e81b94633eacd39 applies when the normalized Euclidean offset is at most 1/sqrt(48). Equivalently, its fit event here would require \(\|B(X-\mu)\|_2^2/a_Z^2\le1/12\). Equation (2) only proves mass at least \([1-(75/2)n/d]_+\) for that event, which gives no positive lower bound when d=n. The fourth estimate clears the coordinate legality issue but does not replace that small-offset cap calculation. Coordinate margin alone cannot do so: for U uniform on [-1/2,1/2]^d and \(\delta=(1/4)\mathbf1_d\), every coordinate has margin 1/4, but Chebyshev's inequality gives \(\mathbb P(\sum_l U_l\ge d/4)\le4/(3d)\). Thus these containing caps can have vanishing mass.

The exact remaining cap test for the combined event proved here is whether there is one constant kappa>0 such that, for every integer d>=1, every \(\delta\in[-1/4,1/4]^d\) with \(\|\delta\|_2\le5/2\), and every nonzero \(v\in\mathbb R^d\),
\(\operatorname{vol}_d\{u\in[-1/2,1/2]^d:v\cdot(u-\delta)\ge0\}\ge\kappa\).
This packet does not use or prove that assertion. In particular, neither the covariance theorem nor the successful inward-coordinate test is presented as a proof of the locked conjecture or as a depth counterexample.
statement:
Let n,d be integers with d>=n>=5, let R>0, and let B be any real d-by-n matrix with |B_li|<=1. For x in R^n define a(x)=R-sum_i |x_i| and c_B(x)=B|x|, where |x| is the vector of coordinatewise absolute values. Define

\[
\begin{aligned}
C_B&=\left\{(x,y):\sum_i|x_i|\le R,\quad
 c_B(x)-a(x)\mathbf 1_d\le y\le c_B(x)+a(x)\mathbf 1_d\right\},\\
D_+&=\left\{z\in\mathbb Z^n:\sum_i|z_i|<R\right\},\qquad
a_z=R-\sum_i|z_i|,\\
C_{B,z}&=c_B(z)+[-a_z,a_z]^d,\qquad
w_z=(2a_z)^d,\qquad W=\sum_{z\in D_+}w_z,\qquad p_z=w_z/W.
\end{aligned}
\]

Vector inequalities are coordinatewise. Then C_B is a compact, full-dimensional convex body, D_+ is its complete positive integer support, and w_z are its actual fiber volumes. The symbols D_+, a_z, w_z, W, p_z, and T_z=2a_z I_d have exactly the same normalizations as in accepted fact 5e81b94633eacd39. That fact's special centroid c_z is replaced here by the actual centroid c_B(z); the radius and volume law are unchanged. In particular, p is the original volume law, not a root-weight law.

For each real k>0 put \(\mathcal Z_k=\sum_{z\in D_+}a_z^k\) and \(q_z^{(k)}=a_z^k/\mathcal Z_k\). The law called q in the assignment is exactly \(q^{(d-2)}\), and its centering vector is \(\mu=\mathbb E_{q^{(d-2)}}|Z|\). In each expectation below Z has the law specified by its subscript.

Every distinct pair of coordinates satisfies \(\operatorname{Cov}_{q^{(k)}}(|Z_i|,|Z_j|)\le0\) for every k>0. Moreover,

\[
\begin{aligned}
\mathbb E_p\!\left[\frac{\|B(|Z|-\mu)\|_2^2}{a_Z^2}\right]
&\le \frac{2n}{(n-1)d(d-1)}\|B\|_F^2
\le \frac{25}{8}\frac nd,\\
\mathbb E_p\!\left[\left(\frac{b\cdot(|Z|-\mu)}{a_Z}\right)^4\right]
&\le \frac{10^{10}}{d^4}\left(\sum_i b_i^2\right)^2
\qquad\text{for every }b\in\mathbb R^n.
\end{aligned}
\]

The fourth estimate in particular applies to every row of B. The point \((0_n,B\mu)\) belongs to \(C_B\cap(\mathbb Z^n\times\mathbb R^d)\). Define

\[
\begin{aligned}
F_B&=\left\{z\in D_+:\|B(|z|-\mu)\|_\infty\le a_z/2\right\},\\
G_B&=\left\{z\in D_+:\|B(|z|-\mu)\|_2^2\le25a_z^2\right\}.
\end{aligned}
\]

With \([t]_+=\max\{t,0\}\), their original-weight fit masses satisfy

\[
\begin{aligned}
p(F_B)&\ge\left[1-16\cdot10^{10}\frac{n^2}{d^3}\right]_+,\\
p(F_B\cap G_B)&\ge
 \left[1-\frac{n}{8d}-16\cdot10^{10}\frac{n^2}{d^3}\right]_+.
\end{aligned}
\]

On every fiber indexed by F_B the constant affine fit Bmu lies at least a_z/2 from each facet. On F_B intersect G_B its normalized offset \(T_z^{-1}(B\mu-c_B(z))\) also has Euclidean norm at most 5/2. All statements hold for every R>0, including R equal to or arbitrarily close to an integer. They make no assertion about arbitrary convex bodies or about the halfspace depth of C_B.
